To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Epstein-Barr virus is frequently detected in whole blood and that its load correlates with HIV surrogate marker levels and the occurrence of non-Hodgin lymphoma in HIV-infected adults.
the Epstein-Barr virus DNA load in whole-blood correlates with HIV surrogate marker and lymphoma, and that Epstein-Barr virus is rarely detected in plasma samples.
EBV DNA load is frequently detected in the whole blood of HIV-infested patients and that it is correlated with surrogate markers of disease.

there is no evidence to support the use of EBV DNA testing in the management of patients with lymphoma.
the EBV DNA load is significantly higher in HIVinfected patients with a CD4 cell count below 200 cells per cubic milliiter.
there are many reasons why a particular person might have a higher EBV viral load than others, and that the viral load is likely to change over time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the whole blood EBV level is more likely to correlate with surrogate markers of disease progression and NHL in HIVinfected adults.
EBV DNA load is not a useful marker for the risk of developing lymphoma.

the EBV load in plasma is not a useful surrogate marker of EBVL disease in HIV-1– infected adults.
